entry.title: 40 Years of Innovation: Rice’s Ken Kennedy Institute Shapes the Future of AI

media:group.media:title: 40 Years of Innovation: Rice’s Ken Kennedy Institute Shapes the Future of AI
media:group.media:description:
For 40 years, Rice University’s Ken Kennedy Institute has brought together researchers across disciplines to advance computing and tackle some of society’s greatest challenges. Today, as artificial intelligence transforms nearly every field, the institute is building on that legacy of collaboration to help shape the future of AI.
From advancing health care and energy innovation to improving flood predictions and urban resilience, Rice researchers are harnessing the power of AI and high-performance computing to develop real-world solutions.
Hear from Rice leaders Lydia Kavraki, university professor and director of the Ken Kennedy Institute; Luay Nakhleh, William and Stephanie Sick Dean of the George R. Brown School of Engineering and Computing; David Sholl, executive vice president for research; and David Pynadath, executive director for research initiatives at the Ken Kennedy Institute, as they reflect on the institute’s legacy, growing impact and commitment to responsible, human-centered AI.
Learn more: https://kenkennedy.rice.edu/

entry.title: Critical Media Lab puts pop lyrics under microscope

media:group.media:title: Critical Media Lab puts pop lyrics under microscope
media:group.media:description:
Students in Rice University’s newest research course spend their semester with pop songs. On a recent afternoon, they spent it teaching an artificial intelligence model to read lyrics the way they do.
The course Critical Media Lab launched this fall as the research arm of Rice’s Program in Media Studies. Under Matthew Schneider-Mayerson, associate professor of English and creative writing and director of the Program in Environmental Studies, students are coding lyrics from songs released since 1990 for environmental themes and related ideas — from plants and animals to consumerism, extreme wealth and excessive heat.
The work began with human readers. Students coded 200 songs by hand, testing each against 60 questions that could apply to any song, story, novel or film.
“Developing the codebook as human coders was the most mind-blowing part,” said Divya Saikumar, a senior majoring in environmental science who is also enrolled in Rice’s master’s program in environmental analysis. “Music is an art, and art is so difficult to interpret. We have to try to tap into the minds of songwriters, and when a single line has a double entendre or multiple meanings, we’ll sometimes spend 20 or 25 minutes asking, ‘What did he actually mean when he said that?’”
The codebook now doubles as a set of instructions. The class is customizing a large language model to extend its coding to more than 50,000 songs, building a representative snapshot of which environmental themes appear in contemporary popular music and which are missing.
“We sometimes talk about AI as if it were a disembodied thing, but it has many different aspects, and it’s a tool like any other technology,” Schneider-Mayerson said. “What’s particularly interesting for students who may not have taken classes in coding or AI is seeing all the ways you can adjust the instructions you give it and how those adjustments lead to different outcomes. Beyond our project, I think that teaches them broader lessons about what these technologies are and how they might use them for good in their own lives.”
The project grew out of a summer research internship Saikumar completed with Schneider-Mayerson, studying how media shapes people’s views of climate change. After weighing podcasts, short stories and film, they chose music because people listen to it constantly, often as background noise. They suspected climate change rarely surfaces in lyrics and wanted to measure how rarely.
“We know that song lyrics can affect our moods and our opinions, but we don’t really know what those lyrics depict or evoke when it comes to the environment and climate change because we’ve never bothered to collect that data,” said Julia Huggins, a media studies lecturer who supports the lab as a researcher. “That’s a gap in the scholarly literature, and these students are working together to fill it. It’s exciting for a group of undergraduates to be working with a professor toward a co-authored publication or a public-facing report that addresses that gap.”
Schneider-Mayerson has published research with previous classes, including studies of climate change in film and in short stories published in The New Yorker. Faculty propose the lab’s research projects, and it typically takes on a new one each semester. Michael Dango, director of the Program in Media Studies, will lead it in spring 2027, and Huggins said the rotation gives media studies majors and minors, as well as students across campus, a chance to take part.
Read full article in Rice News: https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/critical-media-lab-puts-pop-lyrics-under-microscope

entry.title: Inside the Vote: Rice University Opens New Voting Research Center

media:group.media:title: Inside the Vote: Rice University Opens New Voting Research Center
media:group.media:description:
What happens inside a polling place can influence how people vote. At Rice University, researchers are taking a closer look.
The Rice Center for Voting has opened a new simulated polling place equipped with 20 voting stations, allowing researchers to study how waiting lines, polling place layouts and voting technology affect voter behavior.
Faculty and students are examining what encourages voters to check their printed ballots and how their findings could help improve election accuracy, security and the overall voting experience.
The new facility also brings to life the vision of the late Robert “Bob” Stein, a longtime Rice political scientist and former dean of the School of Social Sciences who helped establish the center.
Learn more about research at Rice University: https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/inside-vote-rice-researchers-turn-new-space-laboratory-democracy

entry.title: Two mature oak trees find new home in Rice Village’s future Gateway Park

media:group.media:title: Two mature oak trees find new home in Rice Village’s future Gateway Park
media:group.media:description:
Two towering oak trees that have stood near Rice Village for approximately 70 years have a new home as part of Rice University’s ambitious Gateway Project, which will transform the west side of campus and strengthen connections to the surrounding community. The trees, each approximately 50 feet tall, have been relocated to the site of the future Gateway Park near the corner of Greenbriar Dr. and the planned Amherst roadway extension. The park will be among the first phases of the Gateway Project, a broader initiative announced in November 2025 to create a more pedestrian-friendly connection between Rice's campus and the heart of Rice Village.
Rather than removing the trees and planting replacements, Rice is preserving these mature oaks to serve as natural anchors for the new park. Their established canopies will provide immediate shade, help cool the surrounding area and create a welcoming green space for residents, students and visitors. Additional trees will also be planted as the park takes shape.
The relocation was led by Rice Real Estate Co. in partnership with the Rice Village Management District. Environmental Design Inc. (EDI), a Texas-based company specializing in large-tree relocation, began the process the week of Oct. 5.

entry.title: Student pianist takes on Bartók’s final concerto at Shepherd Spotlight

media:group.media:title: Student pianist takes on Bartók’s final concerto at Shepherd Spotlight
media:group.media:description:
Béla Bartók never heard his final piano concerto. He died in New York in September 1945, 17 bars short of finishing the orchestration, and the work premiered without him the following February. Rice University senior Max Milian will play it with the Shepherd School of Music’s Symphony Orchestra Nov. 7. Milian, a 2026 Shepherd School Concerto Competition winner, is the featured soloist for “Shepherd Spotlight: Bartók 3,” which begins at 7:30 p.m. in Stude Concert Hall.
“It’s an incredibly joyful, beautiful and unique piece,” Milian said. “Many of its sounds can’t be found anywhere else, yet it’s accessible even on a first listen. I think Bartók was searching for happiness at the end of his life, and the piece is full of it.”
Spotlight concerts put students from across the Shepherd School onstage together. Miguel Harth-Bedoya, distinguished resident director of orchestras, leads the program with assistant conductors Kyle Haake, Clayton Hinton and Ana Spasovska, all master’s students in orchestral conducting. The evening opens with the world premiere of “OVERDRIVE,” a piece by recent alumnus Ethan Resnik ’26 inspired by a motorcycle ride through Bangkok, followed by a selection of Mahler’s orchestral songs featuring vocal students Natalie Creel (mezzo-soprano), Nicholas Gryniewski (baritone) and Lewei Wang (baritone).
Milian closes the night. He said he chose the Shepherd School after a lesson with Brian Connelly, artist teacher of piano, while applying to colleges.
“Max entered Rice as an uncommonly gifted and exceptionally well-trained freshman, and now as a senior he continues to astonish us and outdo himself,” Connelly said. “He is amazingly accomplished, voraciously curious about everything and apparently unencumbered with the usual music-student neuroses! He’s also blessed with a really genuine and likable personality.”
Milian said he was also drawn to the culture at the Shepherd School, which he found uniquely friendly and supportive.
Milian said he first encountered the concerto as a freshman, when he came across a recording he loved. Nearly a year ago, he set aside plans to learn Ravel’s Piano Concerto in G for the competition and ultimately chose the Bartók so he could prepare it with Connelly. At the University of Michigan, Connelly had studied with György Sándor, Bartók’s pupil and friend, who gave that 1946 premiere with Eugene Ormandy and the Philadelphia Orchestra.
“I’m sure Mr. Sándor would be delighted to hear how Max captures the many vivid characters of the piece: boisterous and rowdy, meditative and lyrical, wildly virtuosic,” Connelly said. “I feel honored and rewarded to have served as a small connective thread between Bartók’s original vision and Max’s tremendous interpretation.”
For most of the past year, Milian has lived with the concerto’s piano part. Rehearsals with the full orchestra are now underway.
“The orchestration is incredibly exciting,” Milian said. “There are so many colors, and every instrument has something fun to do. I’m really looking forward to hearing it all come together in person.”
Tickets start at $5 and are available at music.rice.edu/events. The concert runs without intermission and will also be livestreamed: https://music.rice.edu/free-live-streams-stude-concert-hall

entry.title: Tragedy, slapstick to share stage in Shepherd School's ‘Ariadne auf Naxos’

media:group.media:title: Tragedy, slapstick to share stage in Shepherd School's ‘Ariadne auf Naxos’
media:group.media:description:
A wealthy patron hires a tragic opera company and a troupe of slapstick comedians for the same evening. Then he orders them to share the stage. The chaos that follows drives Richard Strauss’ “Ariadne auf Naxos,” which Rice University’s Shepherd School of Music will stage this weekend in Morrison Theater at Brockman Hall for Opera.
“My inspiration for this production actually came from being asked to put on a gala at Buckingham Palace in London,” director Paul Curran said. “The experience was nearly identical to the events of this opera.”
Egos collide backstage in the prologue as both companies absorb the patron’s demand. In the opera that follows, the abandoned princess Ariadne mourns on the island of Naxos while a band of comedians tries to cheer her up.
“‘Ariadne auf Naxos’ is a brilliantly crafted work, both hilariously funny and deeply moving,” said conductor Christian Reif, who leads the Shepherd School Chamber Orchestra. “Bringing its contrasting musical styles to life is no small feat.”
“The music is difficult, the German language goes a mile a minute, which is challenging for nonnative speakers, and the amount of dramatic focus and energy required to sustain the theatrical roller coaster is massive,” said Joshua Winograde, director of opera studies at the Shepherd School of Music.
Winograde said the opera would stretch a typical conservatory. The Shepherd School can stage it, he said, because its singers are more advanced technically, musically and dramatically than any student cast he has seen, and because Reif and Curran know the work intimately and hold the cast and orchestra to exacting standards.
Performances are scheduled for 7:30 p.m. Oct. 30 and 2 p.m. Nov. 1. The opera is sung in German with English surtitles. Reif will host a preshow talk in the Tudor Patrons’ Lounge one hour before each curtain, open to ticket holders on a first-come, first-served basis.
Tickets are available on the Shepherd School’s website: https://music.rice.edu/content/strausss-ariadne-auf-naxos

entry.title: The Future of AI at Rice

media:group.media:title: The Future of AI at Rice
media:group.media:description:
Rice University launched AI Week 2026 with a fireside chat focused on how artificial intelligence will shape the university’s future in research, teaching and operations. Moderated by Christopher Jermaine, chair of the department of computer science and Victor E. Cameron Professor of Computer Science, the discussion brought together President Reginald DesRoches, Howard R. Hughes Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs Amy Dittmar and Executive Vice President for Operations, Finance and Support Kelly Fox to explore the opportunities, challenges and institutional responsibilities associated with AI adoption.
The central message was clear: Rice should embrace AI as a transformative tool while preserving the human relationships, academic rigor and personalized educational experience that define the university. Rather than pursuing AI adoption for its own sake, Rice aims to use the technology thoughtfully, responsibly and in ways that advance its academic mission. Programming for AI Week includes more than 30 various panels that centered on the use of AI technology in academia. The week is a cornerstone of Rice’s WISEOwl campaign, a yearlong internal initiative supporting the responsible and effective integration of AI across campus. It bolsters Momentous, the university’s strategic plan that is shaped in part by a call for responsible AI.
Several key themes and discussion points filled the hour-long gathering.
Read more about The Future of AI at Rice in Rice News: https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/ai-fireside-chat-key-takeaways-future-ai-rice

entry.title: At the Moody, mural becomes instrument and gallery becomes stage

media:group.media:title: At the Moody, mural becomes instrument and gallery becomes stage
media:group.media:description:
Double bassist Laura Dykes and wind player Aryn Ward stepped up to a mural at Rice University’s Moody Center for the Arts and began to play it. Their Oct. 10 performance was one half of this season’s Dimensions Variable, the series of live performances and interactive experiences the Moody stages for every fall and spring exhibition. In the neighboring central gallery, Danza Azteca Macuilxochitl presented Mesoamerican dance, music and ceremony, traditions the group carries forward through lineage-based relationships with teachers in Mexico and passes between generations.
Both performances drew from “Radiant Geometries: Vectors of Knowledge from the Indigenous Americas,” an exhibition on the math, science and technology embedded in Indigenous knowledge systems. The mural Dykes and Ward played is a new commission by Diné artist Nanibah Chacon, an interactive sound installation in the Brown Foundation Gallery.
“The wavelengths emitted from this piece are permeable, an ancient technology known and practiced by our ancestors through all cultures,” Chacon said in remarks before the performance. “It is why sound is a part of prayer and capable of healing.”
Dykes and Ward of the Houston nonprofit Nameless Sound put that technology to work with an original score.
“This is something that I’ve dreamed about since creating this piece, allowing for new temporal and experimental work to be experienced,” Chacon said.
Visitors get their turn too. Chacon made the installation for anyone to play, and she said finding its meaning is up to each person who does. “Radiant Geometries” is on view through Dec. 19, and admission is free.

entry.title: Is the electric guitar cool again?

media:group.media:title: Is the electric guitar cool again?
media:group.media:description:
At 15, Chapman Welch was living a musical double life, practicing classical music while playing electric guitar for pay in bars. Those two worlds met Oct. 8-9 at the Adventurous Electric Guitar Festival, which brought guitarists, composers, technologists and students to Rice University’s Shepherd School of Music for two days of concerts, talks and workshops before closing at Dan Electro’s Guitar Bar in the Heights.
Welch, lecturer in music and electroacoustic music specialist at the Shepherd School, co-founded the festival with composer and guitarist Christopher Trapani, assistant professor of experimental music and digital media at Louisiana State University.
“Every year, a consortium of schools from Texas and Louisiana holds a student event, and as the students gather, so do the professors,” Welch said. “We started talking about a guitar festival, and because I have a lot of contacts in the guitar community, we said, ‘Let’s do an adventurous electric guitar festival.’”
LSU hosted the inaugural edition in March 2025. This year, every lecture and concert took place in Houston with support from Rice’s Creative Ventures Fund and Rice Electroacoustic Music Labs, known as REMLABS.
Erik Broess, assistant professor of musicology, opened the festival with a keynote address on the instrument’s reputation. Broess, who studies the culture of guitar tone and gear, grew up idolizing Peter Frampton, Iron Maiden and Rush, and he admitted he once felt like an outsider at a festival with “adventurous” in its name.
“Six strings on an electric guitar serve as the basis for near-infinite variation and creative reinvention,” Broess said in his keynote. “Yet the guitar is also deeply haunted by its past. Outside festivals like this one, the guitar still symbolizes 1960s and 1970s classic rock culture for many people.”
Broess traced how the instrument got its reputation. A symbol of teenage rebellion in the 1950s, Broess said the electric guitar began a long corporate slide in 1965 when CBS bought Fender for $13 million. Vintage guitars once coveted by baby boomers now sell for more than $500,000, and by the 1990s, the instrument had become background music for car and beer commercials. In the 2023 film “Barbie,” a crowd of Kens serenades uninterested Barbies with acoustic guitars around a campfire.
Read the full Rice News article: https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/electric-guitar-cool-again
